nodeData.note: Some bills are paid late and some are paid early, so the cash paid in a year is rarely the true cost of that year. Accruals and prepayments are year-end adjustments that move income and expenses into the year they belong to, so profit and the statement of financial position are correct.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Cash and costs do not always move together. These adjustments fix the gap at the year end, after the trial balance (topic 5) and before the final accounts (topic 6).

children.topic: Cash paid is not the cost
children.note: A duka may pay the December Kenya Power bill in January. The electricity was used in December, so it is a December cost even though the cash left in January.
Changes made at the end of the year, after the trial balance, so each year shows only its own income and expenses. Accruals and prepayments are the most common ones.

manas.q: What is a year-end adjustment?

children.note: Costs owed (accrued expenses), costs paid early (prepaid expenses), income still to be received (accrued income) and income received early (income received in advance).

children.topic: Where it fits in the course
children.note: You record transactions with double entry (topic 3), post them to ledgers and extract a trial balance (topic 5), then make these adjustments before preparing final accounts (topic 6).
Managers, banks, KRA and SACCO lenders rely on profit figures. If a large bill is left out, profit looks better than it really is and decisions are made on wrong numbers.
The basic rule: record income when it is earned and expenses when they are used up, not when cash moves.
Income and expenses are recorded in the period they are earned or used, whatever the date of payment. It is also called the accruals basis of accounting.

manas.q: What does the accruals concept say?

children.note: Expenses are set against the income they helped to earn in the same period, so profit for the year is fair.

manas.q: What is the matching concept?

children.note: Cash basis records only money in and out. Accruals basis records what was earned and used. Proper financial statements, including those under IFRS for SMEs, use the accruals basis.

manas.q: How does the cash basis differ from the accruals basis?

children.note: IAS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements lists the accrual basis as a general feature of financial statements, and IFRS for SMEs follows the same idea. Cash flow statements are the exception.
Most examples here use a year ending 31 December 2025. Always check the year-end date in a question before counting months.
Two are about expenses and two are about income. Each one creates a balance in the statement of financial position.
A cost used up this year but not yet paid at the year end, such as an unpaid December electricity bill. It is added to the expense and shown as a current liability.

manas.q: What is an accrued expense?

children.note: Dr Expense account (e.g. Electricity) / Cr Accruals. This increases the expense and creates a liability.

manas.q: What is the journal entry for an accrued expense?

children.note: Income statement: expense goes up. Statement of financial position: 'Accruals' under current liabilities, often grouped with trade and other payables.
A cost paid this year that belongs to next year, such as insurance paid for months after the year end. It is taken out of this year's expense and shown as a current asset.

manas.q: What is a prepaid expense (prepayment)?

children.note: Dr Prepayments / Cr Expense account (e.g. Insurance). This reduces the expense and creates an asset.

manas.q: What is the journal entry for a prepaid expense?

children.note: Income statement: expense goes down. Statement of financial position: 'Prepayments' under current assets, often with trade and other receivables.
Income earned this year but not yet received, such as December rent owed by a tenant. It is added to income and shown as a current asset.

manas.q: What is accrued income?

children.note: Dr Accrued income (a receivable) / Cr Income account (e.g. Rent received). Income goes up and an asset is created.

manas.q: What is the journal entry for accrued income?

children.note: Income statement: income goes up. Statement of financial position: current assets, as accrued income or other receivables.
Cash received this year for goods or services the business will provide next year. It is taken out of this year's income and shown as a current liability, also called deferred income.

manas.q: What is income received in advance (deferred income)?

children.note: Dr Income account (e.g. Rent received) / Cr Income received in advance (deferred income). Income goes down and a liability is created.

manas.q: What is the journal entry for income received in advance?

children.note: Income statement: income goes down. Statement of financial position: current liabilities, because the business still owes the customer the service.
Owe it = liability (accrued expense, income in advance). Owed to us or already paid for = asset (prepayment, accrued income).

manas.q: Which of the four adjustments are assets and which are liabilities?

children.note: In the ledger, the adjustment appears as a closing balance carried down (c/d) at the year end and brought down (b/d) on the first day of next year.
c/d means carried down: the balance left at the year end. b/d means brought down: the same balance shown again on day one of the next year, on the other side.

manas.q: What do c/d and b/d mean?

children.topic: Accrual sits on the credit side b/d
children.note: In an expense account, an accrual is entered as balance c/d on the debit side and comes back as balance b/d on the credit side. A credit balance is a liability.

children.topic: Prepayment sits on the debit side b/d
children.note: In an expense account, a prepayment is entered as balance c/d on the credit side and comes back as balance b/d on the debit side. A debit balance is an asset.
The figure that makes the account balance after the c/d entry is the true expense or income for the year. It is transferred to the income statement (profit or loss).
Expense = cash paid − opening accrual + closing accrual + opening prepayment − closing prepayment. The ledger account does this for you.

manas.q: What is the formula for the expense charged for the year?

children.note: Some businesses use separate Accruals and Prepayments accounts instead of balances inside each expense account. The result in the final accounts is the same.
Opening balances unwind in the new year so that the cash paid or received is not counted twice.
The December bill accrued in 2025 is paid in January 2026. Without a reversal, that bill would be charged again as a 2026 expense.

manas.q: Why are accruals reversed in the next year?

children.topic: How the b/d balance reverses it
children.note: The opening balance b/d sits on the opposite side of the expense account. When the cash is paid, the two cancel, so only the new year's cost remains.
With a separate accruals account, post on 1 January: Dr Accruals / Cr Expense for the old accrual, and Dr Expense / Cr Prepayments for the old prepayment.
Many packages let you tick 'auto-reverse' on an accrual journal so it reverses on the first day of the next period. Check the reversal date is correct.
A small Nairobi retailer, Wanjiku Stores, with a year ending 31 December 2025. All figures in KES.
Paid Kenya Power bills of KES 42,000 in 2025, covering January to November. The December bill of KES 4,500 arrived in January 2026.
42,000 paid + 4,500 accrued = KES 46,500 charged to profit.
Dr Electricity KES 4,500 / Cr Accruals KES 4,500, being December electricity unpaid at year end.
Debit: Bank 42,000 + Balance c/d 4,500 = 46,500. Credit: Profit or loss 46,500. On 1 Jan 2026: Balance b/d 4,500 on the credit side.
Paid KES 48,000 on 1 April 2025 for a year's fire and theft cover, 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026.
KES 48,000 ÷ 12 = KES 4,000 a month. April–December 2025 is 9 months = 36,000. January–March 2026 is 3 months = 12,000.
Dr Prepayments KES 12,000 / Cr Insurance KES 12,000. Insurance charged in 2025 falls to KES 36,000.
Debit: Bank 48,000. Credit: Profit or loss 36,000 + Balance c/d 12,000 = 48,000. On 1 Jan 2026: Balance b/d 12,000 on the debit side.
Shop rent is KES 25,000 a month. In 2025 the business paid KES 325,000, which includes January 2026 rent paid in late December.
Dr Prepayments KES 25,000 / Cr Rent KES 25,000.

children.topic: Accrued income: rent from a tenant
children.note: A tailor rents a back room for KES 8,000 a month. Only KES 80,000 (10 months) was received in 2025; November and December are unpaid.
Rent earned = 12 × 8,000 = KES 96,000. Received 80,000, so accrued income = KES 16,000.
Dr Accrued income KES 16,000 / Cr Rent received KES 16,000. Rent income in 2025 becomes KES 96,000.
On 1 September 2025 a mobile money agent paid KES 150,000 to advertise on the shop wall for 6 months, September 2025 to February 2026.
KES 150,000 ÷ 6 = 25,000 a month. Earned in 2025: 4 months = KES 100,000. In advance: 2 months = KES 50,000.
Dr Advertising income KES 50,000 / Cr Income received in advance KES 50,000.
Electricity 2026: opening accrual KES 4,500; paid KES 52,000 in 2026, including the December 2025 bill; December 2026 bill of KES 5,200 unpaid.
Debit: Bank 52,000 + Balance c/d 5,200 = 57,200. Credit: Balance b/d 4,500 + Profit or loss 52,700 = 57,200.
Electricity expense for 2026 = 52,000 − 4,500 + 5,200 = KES 52,700. The old KES 4,500 bill is not charged twice.

children.topic: Effect on profit and the SOFP
children.note: Each adjustment changes profit and adds a line to the statement of financial position (SOFP). Using the worked examples, with draft profit of KES 600,000.
Accrued expense lowers profit. Prepayment raises profit. Accrued income raises profit. Income in advance lowers profit.

manas.q: How does each of the four adjustments affect profit?

children.note: Prepayments 12,000 + 25,000 = KES 37,000. Accrued income KES 16,000.
Accruals KES 4,500. Income received in advance KES 50,000.
Each journal has one side in profit and one in the SOFP, so assets still equal capital plus liabilities (topic 2), and the trial balance still agrees.
Most lost marks come from wrong month counts and putting balances on the wrong side.
1 April to 31 December is 9 months, not 8. Write the months out if unsure.
Accrual = liability (credit balance b/d). Prepayment = asset (debit balance b/d). Swapping them misstates both profit and the SOFP.
Questions often give last year's accrual or prepayment. Ignoring it double-counts or misses part of the cost.
If the trial balance note says the figure is already adjusted, do not adjust again. Read the notes under the trial balance carefully.
Accrued income has not been received. It is a receivable, not cash at bank.
In practice, tiny amounts may not be worth adjusting. In the exam, adjust everything the question gives you.
Short questions in KASNEB style. Work them before opening the answer steps.
Telephone paid in 2025 was KES 36,000. Opening accrual KES 2,000; closing accrual KES 3,500. Find the expense.
Start with cash paid: 36,000. Take away the opening accrual (last year's cost): 36,000 − 2,000 = 34,000.
Add the closing accrual: 34,000 + 3,500 = KES 37,500 telephone expense.
Policy paid 1 July 2024, KES 48,000 for 12 months. Renewed 1 July 2025, KES 60,000 for 12 months. Year end 31 December 2025.
Opening prepayment from the old policy: January–June 2025 = 6/12 × 48,000 = KES 24,000.
New policy used in 2025: July–December = 6/12 × 60,000 = KES 30,000. Closing prepayment is also KES 30,000.
Insurance expense = 24,000 + 30,000 = KES 54,000. Prepayment in the SOFP = KES 30,000.
A trainee forgot to accrue KES 10,000 of December casual wages. State the effect.
Profit is overstated by KES 10,000 and current liabilities are understated by KES 10,000. Fix: Dr Wages / Cr Accruals KES 10,000.
A tenant pays KES 12,000 a quarter. In 2025 the business received KES 60,000, which includes the January–March 2026 quarter.
Rent income for 2025 = 60,000 − 12,000 = KES 48,000. Income received in advance of KES 12,000 is a current liability. Dr Rent received / Cr Income in advance KES 12,000.

nodeData.note: Big assets such as vehicles and machines are used for many years, so their cost is spread over those years as depreciation. This map covers the key figures, the straight-line and reducing-balance methods, part-year charges, the journal entries and disposals, with worked examples in KES.

children.topic: What depreciation is and why it matters
children.note: Big items like a matatu or a lab machine help the business for many years. Depreciation spreads their cost over those years instead of charging it all at once.
Things the business owns and uses for more than one year, not for resale: vehicles, machines, furniture, computers, buildings.

manas.q: What is a non-current asset?

children.note: The share of an asset's cost that is used up in one year and charged as an expense in that year.

manas.q: What is depreciation, in plain words?

children.note: IAS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment says the cost of an asset, less what it may be worth at the end, should be shared out in a fair way over the years the business uses it. Small Kenyan entities follow the same idea under IFRS for SMEs.

manas.q: Which standard covers depreciation of property, plant and equipment?

children.note: The asset helps earn income every year it is used, so a part of its cost is matched against each year's income (the accruals idea from topic 7).

manas.q: Which accounting concept is depreciation based on?

children.note: Depreciation is a book entry. No money leaves the bank when it is charged; the cash went out when the asset was bought.
The figure left in the books is unused cost, not what the asset would sell for today.
Land normally lasts for ever, so it is not depreciated. A building on the land is depreciated separately.

manas.q: Is land depreciated?

children.note: Use and wear, time passing, becoming out of date (a new model arrives), or a legal time limit such as a lease.
Every depreciation sum starts with three figures: what the asset cost, what it may be worth at the end, and how long it will be used.
Purchase price plus costs to get the asset ready for use: delivery, import duty that cannot be recovered, installation, testing. Not later repairs.

manas.q: What is included in the cost of a non-current asset?

children.note: What the business expects to get for the asset when it stops using it, after selling costs. Example: an old matatu sold for KES 600,000.

manas.q: What is residual value?

children.note: How long the business expects to use the asset, in years or units of work. It may be shorter than the asset's physical life.

manas.q: What is useful life?

children.note: Cost minus residual value. This is the total that will be charged as depreciation over the useful life.

manas.q: What is the depreciable amount?

children.note: Cost minus accumulated depreciation to date. It is the figure shown for the asset in the statement of financial position.

manas.q: How do you calculate carrying amount?

children.note: Residual value, useful life and method should be checked at least once a year. A change applies from now on; past years are not redone.
Buying or improving an asset is capital spending (added to cost). Routine repairs and fuel are revenue spending (expensed at once).

manas.q: What is the difference between capital and revenue expenditure?

children.note: A method is the pattern for sharing out the cost. Choose the one that best fits how the asset's benefits are used up, and use it consistently.
The same charge every year. Good for assets used evenly, like office furniture.
Annual charge = (cost - residual value) / useful life in years.

manas.q: What is the straight-line depreciation formula?

children.note: Sometimes given as "10% per year on cost": charge = cost x 10% each year, the same every year.
A fixed percentage of the carrying amount each year, so the charge is big at first and smaller later. Good for vehicles and machines that lose value fast.
Charge = rate x carrying amount at the start of the year (cost minus accumulated depreciation).

manas.q: What is the reducing-balance depreciation formula?

children.note: Because each year takes a percentage of what is left, the carrying amount gets smaller but never reaches nil.
Rate = 1 - (residual value / cost) raised to the power 1/n, where n is useful life. Exams usually give you the rate.
The charge follows how much the asset is used, for example kilometres driven or tests run. Charge per unit = depreciable amount / total expected units.
Straight-line when use is even; reducing balance when the asset gives most benefit early. Do not switch just to change profit.

manas.q: When is reducing balance more suitable than straight-line?

children.note: When an asset is bought or sold during the year, the business must decide how much depreciation that year gets. The exam question tells you the policy; read it carefully.
A full year's charge in the year of purchase and none in the year of sale, whatever the dates.

manas.q: What is the full-year depreciation policy?

children.note: Charge only for the months the asset was owned: annual charge x months owned / 12.

manas.q: How is pro-rata (time-apportioned) depreciation calculated?

children.note: Same idea: rate x carrying amount x months / 12 in the part year. Later years use the new carrying amount.
"A full year's charge in the year of acquisition" means full-year. "Charged on a monthly basis" or "time-apportioned" means pro-rata.
Depreciation is never credited to the asset's cost account. It is built up in a separate accumulated depreciation account, so cost stays visible.
Dr Depreciation expense / Cr Accumulated depreciation, with the year's charge.

manas.q: What is the journal entry for annual depreciation?

children.note: A credit-balance account holding all depreciation charged so far on an asset class. It is carried forward year to year.

manas.q: What is accumulated depreciation and what balance does it have?

children.note: A debit-balance expense, closed to the income statement each year like rent or wages (topic 6). It starts at nil each year.
The year's depreciation charge is shown with the other expenses, reducing net profit.

children.topic: In the statement of financial position
children.note: Non-current assets shown as cost, less accumulated depreciation, equals carrying amount.

manas.q: How are non-current assets shown in the statement of financial position?

children.note: Assets fall by the charge, and capital falls by the same amount through lower profit. The equation (topic 2) still balances.
A list of each asset with its cost, date bought, location, method and depreciation to date. It should agree with the ledger totals.
When an asset is sold or scrapped, its cost and depreciation are removed through a disposal account. The balance on that account is the profit or loss on disposal.
Dr Disposal / Cr Asset at cost.

manas.q: What are the four disposal account entries?

children.note: Dr Accumulated depreciation / Cr Disposal, with all depreciation charged on that asset up to the date of sale.
Dr Bank (or Receivables) / Cr Disposal with the sale proceeds. In a part-exchange, Dr Asset (new) / Cr Disposal with the trade-in value.
Balance the disposal account. Debit side bigger = loss (Dr Income statement / Cr Disposal). Credit side bigger = profit (Dr Disposal / Cr Income statement).
Profit or loss = sale proceeds - carrying amount at date of sale.

manas.q: How do you calculate profit or loss on disposal?

children.topic: What profit or loss really means
children.note: It shows that past depreciation was a little too much (profit) or too little (loss). It is shown in the income statement, not as sales.
Every figure here has been checked. Year end is 31 December in each case.
Nyota Shuttles buys a matatu on 1 Jan 2025 for KES 3,600,000. Expected residual value KES 600,000; useful life 5 years.
Dr Depreciation expense 600,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation - matatu 600,000.
Same matatu, but bought on 1 April 2025 and the policy is time-apportioned. It is owned for 9 months in 2025.
Under a full-year policy the 2025 charge would be the full KES 600,000, even though it was bought in April.
A Kisumu hospital laboratory buys a blood analyser on 1 Jan 2025 for KES 1,200,000. Policy: 25% reducing balance.
25% x 900,000 = 225,000. Carrying amount 675,000. Accumulated depreciation 525,000.
The charge falls each year: 300,000, 225,000, 168,750. Straight-line would give the same figure every year.

children.topic: Disposal at a profit: the matatu
children.note: Nyota sells the matatu (bought 1 Jan 2025) on 31 Dec 2027 for KES 1,900,000 cash. Depreciation for 2025-2027 = 3 x 600,000 = 1,800,000.
Dr Disposal 3,600,000 / Cr Matatu at cost 3,600,000. Dr Accumulated depreciation 1,800,000 / Cr Disposal 1,800,000. Dr Bank 1,900,000 / Cr Disposal 1,900,000.
Credits 1,800,000 + 1,900,000 = 3,700,000; debits 3,600,000. Credit side bigger by 100,000: profit. Dr Disposal 100,000 / Cr Income statement 100,000.

children.topic: Disposal at a loss: lab machine
children.note: The analyser is sold on 1 Jan 2028 for KES 450,000. Carrying amount after 3 years = 506,250; accumulated depreciation = 693,750.
Dr Disposal 1,200,000 / Cr Lab equipment 1,200,000. Dr Accumulated depreciation 693,750 / Cr Disposal 693,750. Dr Bank 450,000 / Cr Disposal 450,000.
Credits 693,750 + 450,000 = 1,143,750; debit 1,200,000. Debit side bigger by 56,250: loss. Dr Income statement 56,250 / Cr Disposal 56,250.

children.topic: Tax: wear and tear is different
children.note: For tax, KRA does not accept accounting depreciation. It gives its own allowances on qualifying assets, with rates set in tax law.
When working out taxable profit, accounting depreciation is added back to profit and replaced with the tax allowances.

manas.q: How is accounting depreciation treated when computing taxable profit in Kenya?

children.note: Tax allowances on items like machinery and vehicles. Rates and classes change with the Finance Act, so always check the current KRA rules; this map gives no rates.
Accounts aim to show a fair profit; tax rules aim for one fixed, simple treatment for every taxpayer. So the two figures are rarely the same.
These slips cost marks in KASNEB papers. Check each before you move on.
Depreciation goes to accumulated depreciation, never to the cost account. Cost stays unchanged until disposal.
Reducing balance is a percentage of carrying amount, not cost. Taking 25% of cost every year turns it into straight-line.
Straight-line uses cost minus residual value. Reducing balance ignores residual value in the yearly sum; the rate already allows for it.
Read whether the question wants full-year or pro-rata. Do not charge a part year when a full-year policy is given, or the reverse.

children.topic: Forgetting depreciation in year of sale
children.note: Under pro-rata, charge depreciation up to the sale date before working out profit or loss.
Proceeds from selling a non-current asset are not sales revenue. Only the profit or loss goes to the income statement.
Freehold land is normally not depreciated; split land and buildings before calculating.
Try each question on paper first, then open the steps to check.
A delivery van costs KES 2,400,000, residual value 400,000, useful life 4 years. Find the yearly charge and carrying amount after 2 years.
A printer costs KES 500,000, depreciated at 20% reducing balance. Find the charge for years 1 and 2 and the carrying amount at the end of year 2.
Equipment costing KES 960,000 is bought on 1 Oct 2025. Policy: 10% straight-line on cost, time-apportioned. Year end 31 Dec. Find the 2025 charge.

children.topic: Q4: Profit or loss on disposal
children.note: Equipment cost KES 800,000, accumulated depreciation 500,000, sold for KES 250,000. Find profit or loss and the final entry.
250,000 - 300,000 = loss of KES 50,000. Dr Income statement 50,000 / Cr Disposal 50,000.

maps.title: CA11 · 9. Bad debts and allowance for receivables

nodeData.topic: Bad debts and allowance for receivables
nodeData.note: Some credit customers never pay. This map shows how to write off bad debts, set an allowance for doubtful ones, and show receivables at a realistic amount.

children.topic: What bad debts are and why they matter
children.note: When you sell on credit, some customers never pay. This branch explains why the books must show that honestly.
Selling on credit means the customer owes you. The amount owed sits in trade receivables (debtors), an asset, until they pay.

manas.q: What is a trade receivable?

children.note: A customer may close down, disappear or refuse to pay. Money you will never collect is not really an asset any more.
A debt you are sure you will not collect. IFRS-based exams call it an irrecoverable debt; older books say bad debt.

manas.q: What is a bad (irrecoverable) debt?

children.note: A debt that might not be paid, but you are not yet sure. You keep it on the books but set aside an allowance for it.

manas.q: What is the difference between a bad debt and a doubtful debt?

children.note: If you ignore unpaid debts, profit and assets look bigger than they really are. Owners, banks and KRA could be misled.
Like accruals (topic 7) and depreciation (topic 8), this is a year-end adjustment made after the trial balance to show a true profit.
A few simple rules decide how bad and doubtful debts hit the books.
Do not overstate assets or income. If a debt probably will not be collected, show it at the lower, realistic amount.

manas.q: How does prudence apply to receivables?

children.note: The cost of a bad debt belongs in the same year as the sale that caused it, so the expense is recorded in that year.

children.topic: Write off the bad debts first
children.note: Step one at year end: remove debts that are definitely lost. Only then work out the allowance on what is left.

manas.q: At year end, which comes first: writing off bad debts or the allowance?

children.note: A credit balance that reduces receivables for debts that may not be paid. Older names: provision for doubtful debts, allowance for doubtful debts.

manas.q: What is the allowance for receivables?

children.note: An allowance for one named customer you are worried about, for example a clinic that is months late.

manas.q: What is a specific allowance?

children.note: A percentage of the remaining receivables (after write-offs and after removing specific ones) to cover unknown losses, based on past experience.

manas.q: What is a general allowance and what is it based on?

children.note: The allowance account keeps its balance year to year. Each year you charge or credit only the increase or decrease to the income statement.

manas.q: Which part of the allowance goes to the income statement each year?

children.note: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments asks businesses to allow for credit losses they expect, not just ones that have already happened. Detail comes in later papers.
The double entries you need, written Dr / Cr. Learn these five patterns.
Dr Irrecoverable debts expense / Cr Trade receivables (the customer). The debt leaves the books and the loss hits profit.

manas.q: What is the journal to write off a bad debt?

children.note: Dr Irrecoverable debts expense (or Allowance expense) / Cr Allowance for receivables, with the increase only.

manas.q: What is the journal to increase the allowance for receivables?

children.note: Dr Allowance for receivables / Cr Irrecoverable debts expense (reduces the expense, can even give a credit to profit), with the decrease only.

manas.q: What is the journal to decrease the allowance for receivables?

children.note: Reinstate it: Dr Trade receivables / Cr Irrecoverable debts recovered. Then the cash: Dr Bank / Cr Trade receivables.

manas.q: What are the entries when a written-off debt is later paid?

children.note: Many exams accept one entry: Dr Bank / Cr Irrecoverable debts recovered (or Cr Irrecoverable debts expense). Reinstating first keeps a record of the customer paying.
If a customer with a specific allowance is later written off, write off the debt; next year-end the specific allowance is no longer needed and the allowance falls.
Where each figure goes in the income statement and the statement of financial position.
Show one expense line, irrecoverable debts: write-offs plus increase in allowance (or minus a decrease). Recoveries are shown as income or netted off.

manas.q: What goes in the income statement for bad debts?

children.note: Under current assets: trade receivables less allowance for receivables = net receivables. Only the net figure is the realistic asset.

manas.q: How are receivables shown in the statement of financial position?

children.note: The allowance is a credit balance, but it is a reduction of an asset, not money owed to anyone. Never list it under liabilities.
In a trial balance the allowance appears as a credit, usually the opening (last year's) figure. The year-end adjustment is given as a note.
Uzima Hospital Pharmacy, Kisumu, sells medicines on credit to clinics. Year to 31 Dec 2025. Receivables per ledger KES 840,000. Opening allowance KES 72,000.
Write off: Mwangi Chemist 25,000 and Achieng Clinic 15,000 (both closed). Kilimani Clinic owes 60,000 and is doubtful. General allowance: 5% of the rest.
Total written off 25,000 + 15,000 = 40,000. Dr Irrecoverable debts 40,000 / Cr Trade receivables 40,000. Receivables now 840,000 - 40,000 = KES 800,000.
Kilimani Clinic: specific allowance KES 60,000, the full amount owed.
New allowance 60,000 + 37,000 = 97,000. Opening 72,000. Increase 97,000 - 72,000 = KES 25,000. Dr Irrecoverable debts 25,000 / Cr Allowance 25,000.
Write-offs 40,000 + increase 25,000 = KES 65,000 irrecoverable debts expense for 2025.
Trade receivables 800,000 less allowance 97,000 = net receivables KES 703,000 under current assets.
Uzima Pharmacy, year to 31 Dec 2026. Collection improved, and an old debt came back.
Kilimani paid in full, so no specific allowance. Receivables after write-offs 620,000. General 5% x 620,000 = KES 31,000.
Opening 97,000 less new 31,000 = decrease 66,000. Dr Allowance 66,000 / Cr Irrecoverable debts 66,000. This credit increases profit.
Trade receivables 620,000 less allowance 31,000 = KES 589,000.
Mwangi Chemist, written off in 2025, pays KES 25,000 by M-Pesa in 2026. Dr Receivables 25,000 / Cr Irrecoverable debts recovered 25,000; then Dr Bank 25,000 / Cr Receivables 25,000.
The 25,000 is income in 2026. The receivables account goes up and down by 25,000, so its balance is unchanged.
These slips cost easy marks. Check each before you hand in.
Wrong: 5% x 840,000 = 42,000. Right: write off 40,000 first, then work on what remains. The order changes the answer.
Only the increase or decrease goes to profit. Charging the full 97,000 instead of 25,000 double counts last year's charge.
Take the specific debts out before applying the general percentage, or you allow for Kilimani twice.
It is deducted from receivables in current assets, never shown as a liability.
After writing off, use the lower receivables figure in the statement of financial position too, not the trial balance figure.
An increase is a debit to expense; a decrease is a credit. Ask: is the new allowance bigger or smaller than the old one?
Try each one on paper, then open the steps.
Receivables KES 500,000 before adjustments. Write off 20,000. Allowance 4% of receivables. Opening allowance 15,000. Find the charge and net receivables.
500,000 - 20,000 = 480,000. Dr Irrecoverable debts 20,000 / Cr Receivables 20,000.
4% x 480,000 = 19,200. Increase 19,200 - 15,000 = 4,200. Dr Irrecoverable debts 4,200 / Cr Allowance 4,200.
Receivables after write-offs KES 300,000. Allowance 3%. Opening allowance 12,000. What is the entry?
Dr Allowance 3,000 / Cr Irrecoverable debts 3,000. Net receivables 300,000 - 9,000 = KES 291,000.
A matatu SACCO wrote off KES 18,000 owed by a member last year. He pays it in cash this year. Give the entries.
Dr Receivables 18,000 / Cr Irrecoverable debts recovered 18,000; then Dr Cash 18,000 / Cr Receivables 18,000. The 18,000 is income this year.

nodeData.note: Your cash book and the bank statement both track the same money, but they rarely show the same balance on the same day. A bank reconciliation explains the gap, fixes mistakes in your own books, and proves the bank figure is right. The same idea works for a business M-Pesa Till or Paybill statement.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: You compare two records of one bank account: yours (the cash book) and the bank's (the bank statement). Then you list the reasons they differ until both reach the same true figure.
Your own record of money paid into and out of the bank account. It is written by the business from receipts, cheque stubs and payment slips.

manas.q: What is the cash book (bank column)?

children.note: The bank's record of your account for a period, listing every deposit, payment, charge and the running balance. The bank prepares it, not you.

manas.q: What is a bank statement?

children.note: A short working that starts with one balance, adds and takes away the differences, and ends at the other balance. It shows the two records agree once timing gaps are explained.

manas.q: What is a bank reconciliation statement?

children.note: It catches errors and missing entries, spots fraud or stolen cheques early, and gives the correct bank figure for the statement of financial position. Auditors and lenders expect one every month.

manas.q: Give three reasons for preparing a bank reconciliation.

children.note: Most businesses reconcile at least monthly when the statement arrives. Busy shops, hospitals and SACCOs often reconcile weekly or even daily, using online banking.
The cash book is a book of prime entry (topic 4) and also the Bank ledger account (topic 5). Corrections you find here flow into the trial balance and final accounts (topics 5–6).

children.topic: The mirror: bank view vs your view
children.note: The bank looks at your account from the other side. Money you hold in the bank is an asset to you but a debt the bank owes you, so debits and credits appear reversed.
Money in = debit (left side). Money out = credit (right side). A debit balance means you have money in the bank.

manas.q: In the cash book, which side records money paid into the bank?

children.note: To the bank, your deposit is money it owes you, so it shows deposits as credits and withdrawals as debits. A credit balance on your statement means money in your favour.

manas.q: Why does a bank statement show deposits as credits?

children.note: If you owe the bank, your cash book shows a credit balance and the bank statement shows a debit balance (often marked DR or OD).

manas.q: How does an overdraft appear in the cash book and on the bank statement?

children.note: Think of a mirror: what is on your left (debit) is on the bank's right (credit). Same money, opposite sides.
There are only two kinds of difference: items the bank knows about but you have not recorded yet, and items you have recorded but the bank has not processed yet. Plus errors on either side.
You record a cheque or deposit today; the bank processes it a few days later. Nothing is wrong, the records just have different dates. These go in the reconciliation statement.

manas.q: What is a timing difference in a bank reconciliation?

children.note: Cheques you have written and entered in the cash book, but the payee has not yet banked them, so the bank has not paid them out.

manas.q: What are unpresented cheques?

children.note: Money you paid in and recorded, but the bank has not yet added to your account, for example cash deposited late on the last day. Also called outstanding lodgements or deposits in transit.

manas.q: What are uncredited (outstanding) lodgements?

children.note: Things that appear on the statement first, because the bank did them or received them directly: charges, interest, standing orders, direct debits, direct credits and bounced cheques. You fix these in the cash book.
Mistakes in the cash book (wrong amount, transposed figures, missed entry) are corrected in the cash book. Bank errors are reported to the bank and shown in the reconciliation until fixed.

manas.q: Where do you correct an error made in the cash book, and where do you show a bank error?

children.topic: Items to put in the cash book
children.note: These items are on the bank statement but missing from your books. They are real transactions, so you record them before preparing the statement.
Ledger fees, cheque book fees, EFT fees. Dr Bank charges (expense) / Cr Cash book.
Overdraft interest charged: Dr Interest expense / Cr Cash book. Interest earned on a deposit: Dr Cash book / Cr Interest income.
Regular payments the bank makes for you, such as rent, insurance or a loan instalment. Dr the expense or liability / Cr Cash book.

manas.q: What is a standing order and how is it recorded?

children.note: Money paid straight into your account, such as a customer EFT, RTGS or PesaLink transfer, or a dividend. Dr Cash book / Cr the customer or income.

manas.q: What is a direct credit (credit transfer)?

children.note: A customer's cheque bounced, so the bank took the money back. Dr Receivables (the customer owes you again) / Cr Cash book.

manas.q: How do you record a dishonoured (bounced) cheque?

children.note: Work out the difference and correct only that. Example: supplier cheque of KES 3,600 entered as KES 6,300 means payments are overstated by KES 2,700, so debit the cash book KES 2,700.
Always work in this order. Step 1 makes your cash book correct. Step 2 explains why the correct cash book still differs from the bank statement.
Start with the cash book balance, add receipts the bank shows that you missed, subtract payments and charges you missed, and fix your errors. The result is the adjusted cash book balance.

manas.q: What is Step 1 of a bank reconciliation?

children.note: Start with the bank statement balance, add uncredited lodgements, subtract unpresented cheques, and correct any bank errors. The answer must equal the adjusted cash book balance.

manas.q: What is the format of the bank reconciliation statement (starting from the bank statement)?

children.topic: Which figure goes in the accounts
children.note: The adjusted cash book balance is the true bank figure. Use it in the trial balance and the statement of financial position, not the bank statement balance.

manas.q: Which bank balance appears in the statement of financial position?

children.topic: Starting from the cash book instead
children.note: Some exams start with the adjusted cash book and work to the bank balance. Then reverse the signs: add unpresented cheques, subtract uncredited lodgements.
Practical method: tick every item that appears in both records. Unticked items on the statement go to Step 1; unticked items in the cash book go to Step 2.
Wanjiku Hardware, a duka in Nakuru, reconciles at 31 March. Cash book: debit balance KES 84,500. Bank statement: credit balance KES 101,300.

Opening KES 84,500, less bank charges 1,200, less insurance standing order 6,000, plus customer EFT 15,000, less dishonoured cheque (Otieno) 4,500, plus error correction 2,700. Adjusted balance = KES 90,500.

Dr Bank charges 1,200 / Cr Bank. Dr Insurance 6,000 / Cr Bank. Dr Bank 15,000 / Cr Receivables. Dr Receivables (Otieno) 4,500 / Cr Bank. Dr Bank 2,700 / Cr Payables (cheque 3,600 wrongly entered as 6,300).
Balance per bank statement 101,300. Add uncredited lodgement 9,000 = 110,300. Less unpresented cheques no. 451 (12,800) and no. 453 (7,000) = 19,800. Balance per adjusted cash book = KES 90,500.
Step 1 gives KES 90,500 and Step 2 gives KES 90,500, so the account is reconciled. KES 90,500 is the bank asset in the statement of financial position.
Safari Matatu Co. at 30 June. Cash book: credit balance (overdraft) KES 25,000. Bank statement: debit balance (overdrawn) KES 31,400. Treat overdrafts as minus figures to keep it simple.
Overdraft 25,000, plus bank charges 800, plus overdraft interest 1,600 = 27,400 overdrawn. Less direct credit from a client 5,000. Adjusted balance = KES 22,400 overdrawn.
Balance per bank: overdrawn (31,400). Add uncredited lodgement 15,000 = (16,400). Less unpresented cheques 6,000 = (22,400). Agrees with the adjusted cash book.
The KES 22,400 overdraft is shown as a current liability, not netted against other bank accounts unless there is a right of set-off.

manas.q: Where is a bank overdraft shown in the statement of financial position?

children.note: With an overdraft, a lodgement reduces the amount owed and an unpresented cheque increases it. Using minus signs for overdrawn balances avoids mix-ups.

Many Kenyan businesses collect most sales through a Lipa na M-Pesa Till or Paybill. The M-Pesa business statement is treated just like a bank statement, and the M-Pesa account in your books is treated like a cash book.
Keep a separate ledger account (like a second bank account) for each Till or Paybill. Customer payments are debits; charges and transfers out are credits.

manas.q: How should a business record its Till or Paybill money in the books?

children.note: Downloaded from the M-Pesa business portal. It lists each payment in, each charge and each withdrawal with a transaction code, time and running balance.

manas.q: What is the M-Pesa business statement used for in reconciliation?

children.note: Transaction charges, withdrawals or sweeps to the bank, reversals of mistaken payments, cashier errors (cash sale keyed as M-Pesa) and receipts not entered in the till system.
Charges deducted on withdrawals or payments. Record them: Dr M-Pesa charges (expense) / Cr M-Pesa account. Always use the actual charge on your statement.
Moving Till money to the bank: Dr Bank / Cr M-Pesa. It leaves M-Pesa at once but may reach the bank a day or two later, so it can be an uncredited lodgement in the bank reconciliation.

manas.q: How is a transfer from the M-Pesa Till to the bank recorded?

children.note: A customer paid the wrong Till and the money was sent back. If it was booked as a sale, reverse it: Dr Sales (or Receivables) / Cr M-Pesa account.
M-Pesa is almost real-time, so true timing gaps are rare. They appear mainly at the period end, when the till system closes the day at a different hour from the statement cut-off.

Afya Pharmacy, 31 May. M-Pesa account in books: KES 46,250. Statement shows: 15 withdrawals at an example charge of KES 30 each (450, not a real tariff), a reversal 1,500, a bank sweep 20,000 not booked, a cash sale wrongly keyed as M-Pesa 1,200, and a Till payment not booked 3,000.
46,250 less 450 less 1,500 less 20,000 less 1,200 plus 3,000 = KES 26,100. The M-Pesa statement balance is KES 26,100, so the books now agree. The 1,200 entry is Dr Cash / Cr M-Pesa.
Match the till report to the M-Pesa statement every evening using transaction codes. Small daily checks are far easier than a month of unmatched codes, and they catch staff errors fast.
Most lost marks come from putting an item in the wrong step or using the wrong sign.

children.topic: Unpresented cheques in the cash book
children.note: Wrong. They are already in the cash book; they belong only in the reconciliation statement.
Wrong. Charges are real costs you have not recorded, so they go in the cash book (Step 1).
A credit on the bank statement is good news (money in). Do not treat it like a credit in your cash book.

children.topic: Correcting the full amount of an error
children.note: Only post the difference. Receipt of KES 2,450 entered as KES 4,250 needs a credit of KES 1,800, not 4,250.
The final accounts use the adjusted cash book balance, never the raw bank statement figure.
Exam and real work: use the charges actually shown on the statement or in the question. Tariffs change, so never rely on memory.
Try each question first, then open the answer steps.
Bank charges 500 and a direct credit 8,000 are missing from the cash book. Unpresented cheques 12,000; uncredited lodgement 6,000. Prepare both steps.
50,000 less 500 plus 8,000 = KES 57,500 adjusted cash book balance.
63,500 plus 6,000 less 12,000 = KES 57,500. Both agree.

children.topic: Q2: Find the cash book balance
children.note: Bank statement shows an overdraft of KES 10,000. Unpresented cheques KES 4,000; uncredited lodgement KES 9,000. There are no other items.
The cash book shows a credit balance (overdraft) of KES 5,000.
A customer receipt of KES 2,450 was entered in the cash book as KES 4,250. What is the correction?
Receipts are overstated by 4,250 less 2,450 = KES 1,800. Credit the cash book KES 1,800 (Dr Receivables / Cr Bank).
Classify: standing order, unpresented cheque, dishonoured cheque, late deposit, direct credit.
Cash book (Step 1): standing order, dishonoured cheque, direct credit. Reconciliation statement (Step 2): unpresented cheque, late deposit.

maps.title: CA11 · 11. Correcting errors and the suspense account

nodeData.topic: Correcting errors and the suspense account
nodeData.note: How to find bookkeeping mistakes, hold an unexplained trial balance difference in a suspense account, and fix everything with balanced journals. Ends with the effect on profit and the statement of financial position.

children.topic: What errors are and why they matter
children.note: Bookkeepers are human, so wrong postings happen. This topic shows how to find each kind of mistake and fix it with a journal, so the final accounts tell the truth.
Tired staff, figures read wrongly from a receipt, a posting to the wrong customer, or forgetting to post at all. Even computer systems go wrong when the wrong code is typed in.

children.topic: What the trial balance can check
children.note: The trial balance only tells you whether total debits equal total credits. It cannot tell you whether each amount went to the right account.

manas.q: What does a trial balance agreeing actually prove?

children.note: Some errors leave the trial balance still agreeing; others make it disagree. Only the second family needs a suspense account.

manas.q: What are the two main groups of bookkeeping errors?

children.note: You never rub out or overwrite a wrong entry. You put through a correcting entry in the journal (the general journal from topic 4) with a short explanation.

manas.q: Which book of prime entry is used to correct errors?

children.note: You need double entry (topic 3), the ledger and trial balance (topic 5) and final accounts (topic 6). Bank reconciliation (topic 10) is another way of spotting mistakes.

children.topic: Errors the trial balance does not show
children.note: In these six errors the debit and credit are still equal, so the trial balance agrees. A handy memory aid is the first letters: O, C, P, O, R, C.
A transaction is left out completely: no debit and no credit. The totals still agree because nothing was posted.

manas.q: What is an error of omission?

children.note: A credit sale of KES 6,000 to a hotel was never recorded. Fix: Dr Receivables KES 6,000 / Cr Sales KES 6,000.
The amount is right and the type of account is right, but it went to the wrong person's account, for example the wrong customer.

manas.q: What is an error of commission?

children.note: KES 3,000 paid by Kamau was credited to Kariuki's account. Fix: Dr Kariuki KES 3,000 / Cr Kamau KES 3,000.
The entry goes to the wrong class of account, such as treating a capital item (a non-current asset) as an expense, or the other way round.

manas.q: What is an error of principle?

children.note: A boda boda bought for deliveries for KES 60,000 was debited to Purchases. Fix: Dr Motor vehicles KES 60,000 / Cr Purchases KES 60,000.
The wrong amount is written in the book of prime entry, so both the debit and the credit carry the same wrong figure.

manas.q: What is an error of original entry?

children.note: Electricity of KES 3,200 was entered as KES 2,300 everywhere. Fix the KES 900 gap: Dr Electricity KES 900 / Cr Cash KES 900.
The right accounts and the right amount are used, but the debit and credit are swapped round.

manas.q: What is an error of complete reversal and how is it fixed?

children.note: Cash sales of KES 5,000 were posted Dr Sales / Cr Cash. To fix, post double: Dr Cash KES 10,000 / Cr Sales KES 10,000 (once to cancel, once to record).
Two separate mistakes of the same size cancel each other out, so the totals still match by luck.

manas.q: What are compensating errors?

children.note: Wages were overcast by KES 1,000 (debit too big) and Sales were also overcast by KES 1,000 (credit too big). Fix: Dr Sales KES 1,000 / Cr Wages KES 1,000.
Here the debits and credits are no longer equal, so the trial balance fails to agree. The difference goes into a suspense account until found.
Only one half of the double entry was posted, for example the cash book was written but the expense account was not.

manas.q: What is a single-sided (one-sided) error?

children.note: Both halves were posted to the same side. The trial balance is then out by twice the amount.

manas.q: If an amount is posted to the wrong side of one account, by how much is the trial balance out?

children.note: The debit shows one figure and the credit another, for example Dr KES 4,800 but Cr KES 4,500. The gap is the difference.
A day book or ledger column was added up wrongly. "Undercast" means the total is too small; "overcast" means it is too big.

manas.q: What do undercast and overcast mean?

children.note: Two digits are swapped, such as KES 2,700 written as KES 7,200. If it happens on one side only, the trial balance will not agree.

manas.q: What is a transposition error?

children.note: When digits are swapped the difference always divides exactly by 9. For 7,200 minus 2,700 = 4,500, and 4,500 ÷ 9 = 500, so look for a swap.

manas.q: What clue suggests a transposition error?

children.topic: Balance left off the trial balance
children.note: An account balance was simply not copied into the trial balance, or copied into the wrong column. The ledger itself may be fine.
A temporary holding account for the difference in a trial balance that does not agree. It lets you carry on preparing draft accounts while you hunt for the errors.
A short-term account that holds an unexplained difference. It is not a real asset or liability, and should be zero once the errors are fixed.

manas.q: What is a suspense account?

children.topic: Which side to open it on
children.note: Put the difference on the smaller side so the totals agree. If credits are short, the suspense balance is a credit; if debits are short, it is a debit.

manas.q: On which side of the trial balance is the suspense balance entered?

children.note: Debits total KES 820,000 and credits KES 812,500. Credits are short by KES 7,500, so open a suspense account with a credit balance of KES 7,500.
Only errors that made the trial balance disagree go through suspense. The six "invisible" errors (O, C, P, O, R, C) never touch it.

manas.q: Which errors are corrected through the suspense account?

children.note: Each correcting journal that fixes a one-sided error has suspense as its other half. When all are posted, the suspense account should balance off at nil.
A suspense balance should not stay in the final statement of financial position. If a small amount cannot be traced, management must decide, and auditors will ask about it.
Every correction is a journal entry with a debit, an equal credit and a short note saying why. Getting the method right saves marks.
Date, account to debit, account to credit, the amounts, and a narration (a one-line reason). Debits are written first, credits indented below.

manas.q: What are the parts of a journal entry?

children.note: Ask: what was done? What should have been done? The fix is the entry that turns the first into the second.

manas.q: What is the three-step method for working out a correcting entry?

children.topic: Using suspense as the other half
children.note: For a one-sided error, the missing half goes to the right account and the balancing half goes to suspense.
A note such as "Being rent omitted from rent account" tells the reader and the auditor why the entry was made.
Total debits in each correcting journal must equal total credits, even when suspense is one side. Check this before moving on.
Wanjiru runs a duka in Nakuru. Her trial balance at 31 December 2025 shows debits KES 1,511,400 and credits KES 1,500,000. Draft profit is KES 380,000.
Debits exceed credits by KES 1,511,400 − 1,500,000 = KES 11,400. Credits are short, so suspense opens with a credit balance of KES 11,400.
The sales day book was added up KES 9,000 too low, so Sales was credited too little. Receivables control was right.
Dr Suspense KES 9,000 / Cr Sales KES 9,000. Being sales day book undercast. Profit goes up by KES 9,000.
Rent of KES 4,500 paid by M-Pesa was entered in the cash book but never debited to the rent account.
Dr Rent KES 4,500 / Cr Suspense KES 4,500. Being rent omitted from rent account. Profit falls by KES 4,500.
A delivery motorcycle costing KES 60,000 was debited to Purchases. This is an error of principle, so no suspense.
Dr Motor vehicles KES 60,000 / Cr Purchases KES 60,000. Being capital item wrongly treated as purchases. Profit rises by KES 60,000 (before any depreciation).
Cash book correctly shows KES 2,700 paid to Otieno, but his payables account was debited KES 7,200.
Dr Suspense KES 4,500 / Cr Payables (Otieno) KES 4,500. Being payment over-posted. No effect on profit.

children.topic: Error 5: discount on the wrong side
children.note: Discount received of KES 1,200 was debited to the discount received account instead of credited.
Dr Suspense KES 2,400 / Cr Discount received KES 2,400. Twice the amount: once to cancel, once to record. Profit rises KES 2,400.
A KES 3,000 sale to Kamau was posted to Kariuki's account. Error of commission, so no suspense.
Dr Kamau KES 3,000 / Cr Kariuki KES 3,000. Being sale posted to wrong customer. No effect on profit.
Credit side: opening KES 11,400 + rent KES 4,500 = KES 15,900. Debit side: KES 9,000 + 4,500 + 2,400 = KES 15,900. Balance: nil.
KES 380,000 + 9,000 − 4,500 + 60,000 + 2,400 = KES 446,900. Errors 4 and 6 do not change profit.
Motor vehicles up KES 60,000; payables up KES 4,500; suspense gone. Capital rises with the extra KES 66,900 profit.

children.topic: Effect on profit and financial position
children.note: After the journals, you must restate the draft profit and update the statement of financial position. Look at which accounts each journal touches.
Profit changes only when a journal touches income or an expense account (or cost of sales). Suspense, assets, liabilities and capital do not change profit by themselves.

manas.q: When does a correcting journal change the profit?

children.note: More income or less expense raises profit. Less income or more expense lowers it.
Start with draft profit, add each correction that raises it, subtract each that lowers it, and end with corrected profit.

manas.q: What is the layout of a statement of corrected net profit?

children.topic: Effect on the statement of financial position
children.note: Corrections to assets or liabilities change those lines. Any profit change also flows into capital (owner's equity).

manas.q: How does a profit correction affect the statement of financial position?

children.note: IAS 8 deals with material errors found in a later year: the comparative figures are restated. At Foundation level you mainly fix current-year errors.

manas.q: Which standard covers correcting errors from earlier periods?

children.note: These slips cost marks in KASNEB papers more than the theory does. Read each error twice before you write the journal.
Errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry, reversal and compensating never go through suspense.
A wrong-side or reversed entry needs twice the amount to fix, not just the original amount.
Work out which side is short first. Suspense goes on the short side to make the totals match.
Every journal must have equal debits and credits. If yours does not, a step is missing.
A fix between two balance sheet accounts, like payables and suspense, does not touch profit.
If only a day book total is wrong, the personal accounts may be fine. Ask which ledger actually holds the error.
Try each question yourself, then open the answer steps.
A trial balance shows debits KES 820,000 and credits KES 812,500. What is the suspense balance?
Credits are the smaller side, so suspense is a credit balance of KES 7,500.
A payment of KES 5,670 was posted to the supplier as KES 5,760, but correctly in the cash book. What kind of error is this?
KES 5,760 − 5,670 = KES 90, and 90 ÷ 9 = 10 exactly.
It is a transposition error on one side only, so the trial balance is out by KES 90. Fix: Dr Suspense KES 90 / Cr Payables KES 90.
Electricity of KES 3,200 was recorded as KES 2,300 in the cash book and the electricity account. Correct it and state the profit effect.
Dr Electricity KES 900 / Cr Cash KES 900. Being electricity under-recorded.
Profit falls by KES 900. No suspense, because both sides had the same wrong figure.
Draft profit is KES 250,000. Repairs of KES 15,000 were debited to Equipment. What is the corrected profit?
Dr Repairs KES 15,000 / Cr Equipment KES 15,000. Error of principle.
Repairs is an expense, so profit falls: KES 250,000 − 15,000 = KES 235,000.

nodeData.note: How businesses keep one summary account for all customers and one for all suppliers, and check it against the individual accounts to catch errors and fraud.

children.note: A control account is one summary account in the main (general) ledger that shows the total owed by all customers, or the total owed to all suppliers, in one figure.
A duka selling on credit may have 200 customers. Each has a personal account, but the main ledger only needs one figure: the total all of them owe.
A summary account in the general ledger whose balance should equal the total of all the individual accounts in a separate ledger.

manas.q: What is a control account?

children.note: The separate books holding one account per customer or per supplier. They give the detail; the control account gives the total.

manas.q: What is a subsidiary (personal) ledger?

children.note: The control account for customers who owe the business money (trade receivables). Also called the sales ledger control account.

manas.q: What is another name for the receivables ledger control account?

children.note: The control account for suppliers the business owes money to (trade payables). Also called the purchases ledger control account.

manas.q: What is another name for the payables ledger control account?

children.topic: Where it sits in double entry
children.note: Usually the control account is part of the double entry and goes into the trial balance. The personal accounts are kept as memorandum (detail only) records.

manas.q: Is the control account or the personal ledger part of the double entry?

children.note: Control accounts save time, give quick totals and help catch errors and fraud. They build on the ledger and trial balance (topic 5).

children.topic: Quick total for the trial balance
children.note: You can draw up a trial balance using one receivables figure and one payables figure, without adding up hundreds of accounts first.
If the trial balance does not agree, comparing each control account with its list of balances shows which ledger holds the mistake.

manas.q: How do control accounts help locate errors?

children.note: If a different person keeps the control account from the person who keeps customer accounts, one person cannot easily hide stolen cash by changing records.

manas.q: How do control accounts help prevent fraud?

children.note: In a hospital pharmacy one clerk can post patient-company accounts while the accountant keeps the control account. Work is shared and checked.
The owner sees at a glance how much is owed in and owed out, which helps plan cash and chase slow payers.
Control accounts are posted from the totals in the books of prime entry (topic 4), while personal accounts are posted from each single item.
Total credit sales for the month go to the debit of the receivables control account. Each invoice goes to the customer's own account.
Total credit purchases for the month go to the credit of the payables control account. Each invoice goes to the supplier's account.
Sales returns (returns inwards) reduce receivables. Purchases returns (returns outwards) reduce payables.
Money received from credit customers, money paid to suppliers, and the discount columns all come from the cash book.
Unusual items such as bad debts written off, contra entries and corrections are recorded in the journal first.

children.topic: Rule: totals to control, items to personal
children.note: The control account gets the period totals; the personal ledger gets the same amounts item by item. Both should end at the same figure.

manas.q: What is posted to the control account and what to the personal ledger?

children.note: Think of it as one big customer account. Things that increase what customers owe go on the debit side; things that reduce it go on the credit side.
Opening debit balance, credit sales, dishonoured (bounced) cheques, interest charged on overdue accounts, refunds paid to customers.

manas.q: What goes on the debit side of the receivables control account?

children.note: When a customer's cheque bounces, the customer owes the money again: Dr Receivables control / Cr Bank.
If you charge a late customer interest, they owe more: Dr Receivables control / Cr Interest received.
Cash and bank received, discounts allowed, sales returns, bad debts written off, contra entries, closing debit balance carried down.

manas.q: What goes on the credit side of the receivables control account?

children.note: A reduction given to a customer for paying early. Dr Discount allowed (expense) / Cr Receivables control.

manas.q: What is the entry for discount allowed?

children.note: Goods sent back by a customer reduce what they owe: Dr Sales returns / Cr Receivables control.
A debt you will never collect is removed (topic 9): Dr Bad debts expense / Cr Receivables control.

manas.q: What is the entry for writing off a bad debt?

children.note: A customer who overpaid has a credit balance. It is shown as a separate closing credit balance, not netted off, in a full control account.
Think of it as one big supplier account. Things that increase what you owe go on the credit side; things that reduce it go on the debit side.
Opening credit balance, credit purchases, interest charged by suppliers, refunds received from suppliers.

manas.q: What goes on the credit side of the payables control account?

children.note: Cash and bank paid to suppliers, discounts received, purchases returns, contra entries, closing credit balance carried down.

manas.q: What goes on the debit side of the payables control account?

children.note: A reduction a supplier gives you for paying early. Dr Payables control / Cr Discount received (income).

manas.q: What is the entry for discount received?

children.note: Goods you send back to a supplier reduce what you owe: Dr Payables control / Cr Purchases returns.
If you overpaid a supplier, that supplier owes you. Show it as a separate debit balance.
When the same person is both a customer and a supplier, the two balances can be set off against each other so only the net amount is settled.
Cancelling an amount owed to a supplier against an amount the same person owes you, so less cash changes hands.

manas.q: What is a contra (set-off) entry?

children.note: Dr Payables control / Cr Receivables control with the smaller of the two balances. Both totals go down by the same amount.

manas.q: What is the double entry for a contra?

children.note: Otieno buys maize flour from your duka (owes you KES 12,000) and sells you sugar (you owe him KES 20,000). Set off 12,000; you then pay him KES 8,000.
Get the other party to agree the set-off in writing so both sets of books record the same amount.

children.topic: Reconciling with the list of balances
children.note: At month end, list every customer (or supplier) balance and add them up. The total should equal the control account balance. If not, find and fix the errors.
Total both sides and find the closing balance carried down.

children.topic: Step 2: list and total personal balances
children.note: Add up each customer's or supplier's closing balance from the personal ledger.
If they agree, good. If not, there is at least one error in the control account, the personal ledger, or both.
Adjust the control account for errors in totals or postings to it. Adjust the list for errors in single personal accounts. Both corrected figures must agree.

manas.q: In a control account reconciliation, which errors change the control account and which change the list?

children.topic: Errors that affect only the control
children.note: A day book added up wrongly (undercast or overcast), or a total never posted to the control account.

children.topic: Errors that affect only the list
children.note: One invoice posted to the wrong amount in a personal account, a balance left off the list, or an item posted to the wrong side.
An invoice missing from the day book completely, or posted to the wrong customer, leaves both totals still agreeing. Agreement is not proof of no errors.

manas.q: Name an error a control account reconciliation will not reveal.

children.note: Mama Njeri Wholesalers, Nairobi, March 2026. All figures in KES. Each account below balances.
Mama Njeri's receivables control account for March, built from her books of prime entry.
Balance b/d 120,000; credit sales 450,000; dishonoured cheque 8,000. Debit total 578,000.
Bank received 380,000; discounts allowed 9,000; sales returns 15,000; bad debts 6,000; contra 12,000. Subtotal 422,000.
Balance c/d = 578,000 − 422,000 = 156,000. Credit side total then equals 578,000. Customers owe KES 156,000.
Mama Njeri's payables control account for the same month.
Balance b/d 90,000; credit purchases 300,000. Credit total 390,000.
Bank paid 260,000; discounts received 5,000; purchases returns 7,000; contra 12,000. Subtotal 284,000.
Balance c/d = 390,000 − 284,000 = 106,000. Debit total then equals 390,000. She owes suppliers KES 106,000.
Her control account shows 156,000 but the list of customer balances adds up to 149,500. Four errors are found.
Sales day book overcast by 5,000: Cr control 5,000. Discount allowed 1,000 not posted to control: Cr control 1,000. Corrected control = 156,000 − 6,000 = 150,000.
Customer balance 2,000 left off the list: add 2,000. A 750 return debited instead of credited: deduct 1,500. Corrected list = 149,500 + 2,000 − 1,500 = 150,000.
Corrected control 150,000 = corrected list 150,000. The figure for receivables in the trial balance is KES 150,000.
Examiners like to slip in items that do not belong in a control account. Know them well.
Leave them out. They never create a customer or supplier balance, so they never touch a control account.

manas.q: Do cash sales go in the receivables control account?

children.note: The allowance (provision) for doubtful debts is kept in its own account, not in the control account (topic 9). Only actual bad debts written off go in.

manas.q: Does a change in the allowance for receivables go in the control account?

children.note: Usually recorded as Dr Bank / Cr Bad debts recovered, often passing through the control account first. Read the question's method carefully.
A trade discount is taken off the price before the invoice is written, so it is never recorded. Only settlement (prompt-payment) discounts appear.

manas.q: Is trade discount recorded in a control account?

children.note: Discount allowed goes in receivables control; discount received goes in payables control. Swapping them is a classic slip.
Always Dr payables control and Cr receivables control. Both balances fall; never increase either.
Under IFRS 15 a prompt-payment discount you expect the customer to take reduces revenue. Exam questions at this level usually still use the simple discount-allowed entry.

Opening 64,000; credit sales 210,000; received 180,000; discounts allowed 4,000; returns 6,000; bad debts 3,000; contra 2,000. Find closing balance.
Opening 64,000 + credit sales 210,000 = 274,000.
Closing debit balance = 274,000 − 195,000 = KES 79,000.
Opening 45,000; credit purchases 150,000; paid 130,000; discounts received 2,500; purchases returns 3,500; contra 2,000. Find closing balance.
Opening 45,000 + purchases 150,000 = 195,000.
Closing credit balance = 195,000 − 138,000 = KES 57,000.

The credit note is in the personal account, so the list is right. The control account is missing it.
Dr Sales returns 1,400 / Cr Receivables control 1,400. Control becomes 82,000 − 1,400 = 80,600.
Corrected control 80,600 = list 80,600. They now agree.
From this list pick what does NOT go in receivables control: cash sales, discount allowed, allowance for receivables increase, contra.
Exclude cash sales and the allowance increase. Discount allowed and contra both go on the credit side.

nodeData.note: How to value the stock a business holds, using IAS 2: lower of cost and net realisable value, FIFO or weighted average, and how closing stock gives cost of sales.

children.topic: What inventory is and why it matters
children.note: Inventory (stock) is goods a business holds to sell or to use up making things. Getting its value right decides the profit figure and the current assets on the balance sheet.
The things on the shelves waiting to be sold: sugar and soap in a duka, medicines in a hospital pharmacy, spare parts in a garage.

manas.q: What is inventory?

children.note: Goods bought to resell; raw materials and parts waiting to be used in making; and work in progress or finished goods made by the business itself.
Closing inventory is taken away from purchases to get cost of sales. If it is wrong, gross profit and net profit are wrong by the same amount.
Closing inventory goes in two places: deducted in cost of sales in the income statement, and shown as a current asset in the statement of financial position.
Builds on final accounts of a sole trader (topic 6), where opening and closing inventory first appear, and on accruals (topic 7): we match the cost of goods sold to the sales they earned.
IAS 2 Inventories is the IFRS standard on how to value stock. Small Kenyan entities using IFRS for SMEs follow a section with almost the same rules.
Value inventory at whichever is lower: what it cost you, or what you can realistically get for it after selling costs. Never value it above cost.

manas.q: What is the basic valuation rule in IAS 2?

children.note: Net realisable value is the expected selling price less any costs to finish the item and costs needed to sell it.

manas.q: How is net realisable value (NRV) calculated?

children.note: It stops a business showing profit it has not yet earned. A loss you can already see (damaged or expiring stock) is recognised now.

children.topic: Item by item, not in total
children.note: Compare cost and NRV for each item (or group of similar items) separately. A gain on one product must not hide a loss on another.

manas.q: Is the cost vs NRV comparison done in total or item by item?

children.note: Common causes: damage, expiry dates near (medicines), goods going out of fashion, selling prices falling, or high costs still needed to sell.
The drop to NRV is an expense of the period, usually put in cost of sales: Dr Cost of sales / Cr Inventory.

manas.q: What is the double entry to write inventory down to NRV?

children.note: Many small Kenyan businesses report under IFRS for SMEs. Its inventory section also uses lower of cost and selling price less costs to complete and sell.
Cost is everything spent to get the goods to their present place and condition, ready to sell. Some costs must be left out.
Purchase price, import duty and non-refundable taxes, carriage inwards (transport to your store), handling, and for a maker, direct labour and production overheads.

manas.q: What costs are included in the cost of inventory?

children.note: Trade discounts, rebates and similar reductions lower the cost of the goods. Refundable VAT you can claim back from KRA is not part of cost.
Storage after the goods arrive (unless needed in production), selling and advertising costs, general admin overheads, and abnormal waste.

manas.q: Name costs excluded from inventory cost.

children.note: Carriage inwards (bringing goods in) is part of cost. Carriage outwards (delivering to customers) is a selling expense, never part of inventory.

manas.q: Is carriage outwards part of inventory cost?

children.note: A manufacturer adds a share of factory overheads (factory rent, machine depreciation) based on normal output, not on a slow or unusually busy month.
When identical items are bought at different prices, we need a rule for which cost goes out with each sale. IAS 2 allows FIFO or weighted average.
Used for unique, costly items like cars or land plots: each item keeps its own actual cost.
Assume the oldest stock is sold first. Closing inventory is valued at the most recent purchase prices.

manas.q: What does FIFO assume?

children.note: Each unit is valued at the average cost of all units available. Average = total cost of units ÷ number of units.

manas.q: How is weighted average cost calculated?

children.note: A new average is worked out after every purchase. Sales are costed at the average at that moment.
One average for the whole period: total cost of opening stock plus purchases ÷ total units. Simpler, but gives a slightly different answer.
Last in, first out is banned under IFRS and IFRS for SMEs. KASNEB may still ask about it, but your answer should say it is not permitted.

manas.q: Is LIFO allowed under IAS 2?

children.note: When prices rise, FIFO gives a higher closing stock and higher profit than AVCO, because the cheaper old stock is charged to cost of sales first.
Use the same method for inventories of a similar nature and use, and do not switch from year to year without a good reason.
A business can track stock all the time (perpetual) or only count it at the end (periodic).
Purchases go to a purchases account. Stock is counted at period end and cost of sales is worked out as a balancing figure. Common in small dukas.

manas.q: What is a periodic inventory system?

children.note: Every receipt and issue updates the stock record straight away, so stock and cost of sales are always known. Common with tills and pharmacy software.

manas.q: What is a perpetual inventory system?

children.note: The record for each item showing receipts, issues and balance in units and KES, under FIFO or AVCO.
Opening inventory + purchases (plus carriage in, less returns out) − closing inventory = cost of sales.

manas.q: What is the cost of sales formula?

children.note: In a periodic system at year end: Dr Inventory (balance sheet) / Cr Cost of sales (income statement) with the closing value. It becomes next year's opening stock.
Counting what is physically on the shelves. Even with perpetual records, a count is needed to find theft, breakage and recording errors.
Extra points that often turn up in exam questions on closing inventory.
If stock is counted a few days after the year end, adjust back to the year-end date using what happened in between.

manas.q: How do you adjust a stock count taken after the year end?

children.note: Goods sold after the year end were still on the shelves at the year end. Add back their cost (not selling price) to the count.
Goods received after the year end were not there at the year end. Deduct them from the count.
When the owner takes stock for personal use, at cost: Dr Drawings / Cr Purchases. It is not a sale and is not a business expense.

manas.q: What is the entry for goods taken by the owner?

children.note: Goods sent to a customer on sale or return still belong to you until accepted. Include them in your inventory at cost.
Count it separately and write it down to NRV, which may be nil for expired medicines.
All figures checked: each answer adds up.
Hospital pharmacy, paracetamol boxes, January. Opening 100 @ KES 200. Buy 200 @ 230 on 5th. Sell 250 on 10th. Buy 150 @ 250 on 20th. Sell 120 on 28th. 80 boxes left.
80 boxes @ 250 = KES 20,000. Check: 83,500 + 20,000 = 103,500, the total cost of all goods available.
One average: 103,500 ÷ 450 boxes = 230. Closing 80 × 230 = 18,400; cost of sales 85,100.
Sales 250 @ 350 + 120 @ 380 = 133,100. Gross profit: FIFO 49,600; perpetual AVCO 49,000. Prices rose, so FIFO shows more profit.
Duka year: opening stock 120,000, purchases 850,000, carriage in 15,000, returns out 25,000, owner took goods 10,000, closing stock 140,000. Cost of sales = KES 810,000.
Sales 1,200,000 − cost of sales 810,000 = gross profit KES 390,000.
Dr Drawings 10,000 / Cr Purchases 10,000. Net purchases fall to 840,000 before carriage and returns.
Imported stock: price 500,000, trade discount 25,000, import duty 40,000, transport to store 15,000, storage later 8,000, advertising 12,000. Cost = 500,000 − 25,000 + 40,000 + 15,000 = KES 530,000.

children.topic: Why two costs are left out
children.note: Storage after arrival (8,000) and advertising (12,000) are expenses of the period, not part of the stock's cost.

children.topic: Example 4: lower of cost and NRV
children.note: Item A cost 40,000, NRV 55,000 → 40,000. Item B cost 30,000, sells for 22,000 less 2,000 costs, NRV 20,000 → 20,000. Item C cost and NRV 25,000 → 25,000. Value KES 85,000.
Total cost 95,000 − value 85,000 = 10,000. Dr Cost of sales 10,000 / Cr Inventory 10,000.
Total NRV is 100,000, above cost, but the loss on item B must still be recognised. Item by item gives 85,000.
Year end 31 Dec; count on 3 Jan at cost 260,000. Sales 1–3 Jan were 40,000 at selling price with 25% margin, so cost 30,000. Goods received 1–3 Jan 18,000.
Watch for these; they cost marks.
Stock is valued at cost (or NRV if lower), never at selling price. Remove the profit element first.
Margin is profit as a % of selling price; mark-up is profit as a % of cost. 25% margin means cost is 75% of sales; 20% mark-up means cost = sales ÷ 1.2.

manas.q: What is the difference between margin and mark-up?

children.note: LIFO is not permitted under IFRS. If asked, explain it and state that it cannot be used.
Carriage outwards, advertising and shop staff wages are not inventory cost.
If closing stock is overstated by 10,000, this year's profit is overstated by 10,000 and next year's profit is understated by 10,000.

manas.q: What is the effect of overstating closing inventory?

children.note: Goods taken by the owner are recorded at cost to drawings, not as sales.
